content: Motor vehicle (MV) collisions involving animals on roadways are a significant cause of both fatal and nonfatal injuries. These incidents include direct collisions with animals or crashes resulting from drivers attempting to avoid animals. To better understand the nature of nonfatal injuries from such events, the CDC analyzed data from the National Electronic Injury Surveillance System-All Injury Program (NEISS-AIP). This system collects data from a representative sample of U.S. hospital emergency departments (EDs) and provides national estimates of injury cases. The analysis revealed that MV-animal crashes often involve larger animals such as deer, moose, elk, bears, horses, and cattle. Smaller animals like dogs, cats, and raccoons were included only in the overall national estimates. Injuries from these crashes were most frequently head and face contusions, abrasions, or lacerations, as well as neck sprains or strains. A significant proportion of these injuries occurred during October and November, coinciding with the fall deer hunting, mating, and migration season. Crashes were more likely to occur during early morning hours or at dusk, when animal activity is heightened. Preventive measures, such as fencing, underpasses, and improved driver awareness, are recommended to reduce the risk of MV-animal collisions. Additionally, driving within speed limits, staying alert, and avoiding distractions or impaired driving can help drivers react more effectively to potential hazards. Universal use of safety restraints, including seat belts and child safety seats, is critical to minimizing injury severity in the event of a crash. In correctional facilities, hepatitis B virus (HBV) infection is a major public health concern due to the high prevalence of infectious diseases among incarcerated individuals. Studies have shown that the prevalence of current or past HBV infection among adult prison inmates ranges from 13% to 47%, significantly higher than in the general population. HBV transmission can occur both in the community and within correctional settings. A retrospective investigation in Georgia correctional facilities identified ongoing HBV transmission, emphasizing the need for vaccination programs in these environments. The study found that most HBV infections among inmates were acquired during incarceration, with frequent transfers between facilities contributing to the spread of the virus. A prevalence survey conducted at intake centers revealed that a majority of inmates were susceptible to HBV infection, and many consented to vaccination when offered. Despite the demonstrated effectiveness of vaccination programs in reducing HBV transmission, most state correctional systems, including Georgia, lack routine HBV vaccination initiatives. Implementing such programs nationwide could significantly reduce the burden of HBV-associated disease, both within correctional facilities and in the broader community, as inmates are released. The use of tumor necrosis factor-alpha (TNF-α) antagonists, such as infliximab, etanercept, and adalimumab, has been associated with an increased risk of tuberculosis (TB) reactivation. These medications, approved for treating autoimmune diseases like rheumatoid arthritis, work by blocking TNF-α, a cytokine critical to the immune response against TB. Blocking TNF-α can allow latent Mycobacterium tuberculosis infections to progress to active disease. Case reports from California highlighted instances of TB disease in patients receiving infliximab therapy. These cases underscore the importance of TB prevention and management in immunocompromised patients. Healthcare providers should screen for latent TB infection before initiating TNF-α antagonist therapy and remain vigilant for signs of TB, such as unexplained fever or weight loss, during treatment.
